notes: The tools an AI client can call on a Deskway computer (docs/architecture.md, "MCP and tools"). The one definition: crates/wire reads it at build time, the computer implements exactly these (host/src/tools) and the deskway command lists them to MCP clients before it reaches any computer.

batch: the batch a tool comes in. screen: none, read (looks at the screen) or act (changes what the screen shows); an act is refused on a secure desktop. needs_user: the tool requires an available workspace user. Every tool also takes `computer`, added by the deskway command, which picks the computer and is not passed on.

tools.name: computer_info
tools.description: What this computer is and what it allows now: its name and system, its displays, who is signed in, whether it is locked, whether a person is controlling it too, and what an AI client may do here.

tools.name: audit_read
tools.description: What AI clients did on this computer, from its own record, as calls: when each started (unix seconds), the AI client, its device and session, the tool, its arguments, its result (ok, running, or the error's code) and the result in short, and how long it took. Newest first, a page at a time: total says how many fit, clients and tools what the record holds. Records cannot be changed or removed; about the last 8 MB are kept.

since.description: Only calls started at or after this time (unix seconds).

until.description: Only calls started at or before this time (unix seconds).

client.description: Only this AI client's calls, by its name (any case).

failed.description: Only calls that ended in an error.

offset.description: Skip this many first (default 0): the next page is offset + limit.

tools.name: screenshot
tools.description: A picture of one display of the computer (JPEG). The positions the pointer tools take are in this picture's pixels, so take one before pointing, and again after the screen changes.

display.description: The display's id, as computer_info lists them; the primary display by default.

max_width.description: At most this many pixels wide (default 1280, at most 1920); smaller is faster and cheaper to read.

tools.name: wait_for
tools.description: Waits until a display changes, or until it holds still, at most timeout_ms; cheaper than taking screenshots in a loop. Use it after starting something slow (a program opening, a page loading), then take a screenshot. A clock or a blinking cursor on the display counts as change.

until.description: change (default): until it differs from how it looked when the wait began; still: until it has not changed for still_ms.

display.description: The display's id, as computer_info lists them; the primary display by default.

still_ms.description: With until still: how long it must hold still (default 1000, 200 to 10000).

timeout_ms.description: How long to wait at most (default 10000, at most 60000).

tools.name: click
tools.description: Clicks at a place of the latest screenshot.

x.description: Pixels from the left of the latest screenshot.

y.description: Pixels from the top of the latest screenshot.

count.description: 2 for a double click; 1 by default.

tools.name: move
tools.description: Moves the pointer to a place of the latest screenshot, without clicking (to show a tooltip or a menu).

x.description: Pixels from the left of the latest screenshot.

y.description: Pixels from the top of the latest screenshot.

tools.name: drag
tools.description: Presses at one place of the latest screenshot, moves to another and lets go there.

x.description: Pixels from the left of the latest screenshot.

y.description: Pixels from the top of the latest screenshot.

to_x.description: Where to let go, from the left.

to_y.description: Where to let go, from the top.

tools.name: scroll
tools.description: Scrolls with the wheel over a place of the latest screenshot.

x.description: Pixels from the left of the latest screenshot.

y.description: Pixels from the top of the latest screenshot.

tools.name: key
tools.description: Presses a key or a combination, such as Enter, Escape, Tab, ctrl+c, ctrl+shift+t, alt+f4, cmd+space or win+r.

keys.description: Keys joined by +: modifiers (ctrl, shift, alt, cmd or win) and one key (a letter, a digit, Enter, Escape, Tab, Backspace, Delete, Space, Up, Down, Left, Right, Home, End, PageUp, PageDown, F1 to F12).

tools.name: type
tools.description: Types text where the focus is, as it is, whatever the computer's keyboard layout.

tools.name: run
tools.description: Runs a command as the workspace user (the host user on Linux) and waits up to wait_ms. Windows prefers PowerShell 7 and falls back to Windows PowerShell. Ordinary commands on macOS and Linux use $SHELL -lc, defaulting to /bin/zsh and /bin/sh respectively. Programs outlive the AI session. Use proc_read with the returned id and next to read on.

command.description: What to run, as typed in that shell.

cwd.description: The folder to run it in; the shell's default otherwise.

wait_ms.description: How long to wait for it to end (default 30000, at most 600000).

elevated.description: Requires Allow administrator rights. Windows uses the signed-in user's administrator rights. macOS prompts for each elevated run. Linux refuses elevation.

tools.name: proc_start
tools.description: Starts a terminal as the workspace user (the host user on Linux). Windows prefers PowerShell 7 and falls back to Windows PowerShell. macOS and Linux use $SHELL -lc for a command or $SHELL -l for an interactive shell, defaulting to /bin/zsh and /bin/sh respectively. Use proc_write for input and proc_read for plain output. The program outlives the AI session.

command.description: What to run, as typed in that shell; a shell of its own when left out.

elevated.description: Windows only, with Allow administrator rights and the signed-in user's administrator rights. macOS and Linux refuse elevated terminals.

tools.name: proc_write
tools.description: Types into a program proc_start started: text, then keys by name. A line is entered with keys ["enter"]. Then proc_read from the next it answers, with wait_ms, to see what it said.

keys.description: Keys after the text: enter, tab, backspace, escape, up, down, left, right, home, end, delete, ctrl+c, ctrl+d, ctrl+z, ctrl+l.

tools.name: proc_read
tools.description: What a program started with run or proc_start printed (its output and errors together; a terminal's without its colours and cursor moves), from the byte offset `from` on: pass the `next` of the last answer to read on. With wait_ms it waits for something new (or the program's end) first. The last 1 MiB is kept; earlier_output_lost says when bytes before `from` are gone.

id.description: The program's id, from run, proc_start or proc_list.

wait_ms.description: Wait at most this long for output past `from` (default 0, at most 30000).

tools.name: proc_kill
tools.description: Ends a program started with run, and every program it started.

tools.name: proc_list
tools.description: The programs AI clients started on this computer that it still keeps: id, command, running or its exit code, and how much they printed.

tools.name: fs_list
tools.description: The entries of a folder: name, kind (file, folder, link), size and modified time (Unix seconds); at most 2000.

path.description: A full path on the computer.

tools.name: fs_stat
tools.description: One file or folder: kind, size and modified time.

path.description: A full path on the computer.

tools.name: fs_read
tools.description: Part of a file: at most length bytes from offset (default and most 256 KiB). UTF-8 comes back as text, anything else as base64; more and next say how to read on.

path.description: A full path on the computer.

tools.name: fs_write
tools.description: Writes a file, creating it and its folders if needed: text, or bytes as base64. It replaces the file, or appends to it.

path.description: A full path on the computer.

base64.description: The content as base64 bytes, instead of text.

append.description: Add to the end instead of replacing (default false).

tools.name: fs_hash
tools.description: A file's SHA-256 and size: to tell whether two copies are the same, or whether it changed.

tools.name: fs_move
tools.description: Moves or renames a file or folder.

tools.name: fs_delete
tools.description: Deletes a file, or a folder: an empty one, or with everything in it when recursive.

path.description: A full path on the computer.

recursive.description: Delete a folder with what is in it (default false).

tools.name: clipboard_get
tools.description: The text on the computer's clipboard (null when it holds no text).

tools.name: clipboard_set
tools.description: Puts text on the computer's clipboard.

tools.name: tunnel
tools.description: Makes a port of the computer's own loopback (127.0.0.1) reachable from the machine you run on: a web server, a debugger or a database started there. Only a port something listens on now; never another machine. The answer says the local port to connect to here; the tunnel lasts while you use this computer (release, or 10 idle minutes, ends it).

port.description: The port on the computer's loopback.

tools.name: windows
tools.description: The windows open on the person's screen: id, title, app (its program's file name), pid, position and size in screen coordinates (not a screenshot's pixels), and whether minimized, maximized or focused.

tools.name: window_act
tools.description: Does one thing to a window windows listed: focus (brings it to the front), minimize, maximize, restore, close (as its close button would: it may ask about unsaved work), or move (its top left corner to x, y in screen coordinates, and its size to w, h when given).

id.description: The window's id, as windows lists it.

x.description: move: where its left edge goes.

y.description: move: where its top edge goes.

w.description: move: its width, with h; its size stays otherwise.

tools.name: app_list
tools.description: The apps the person can open (Windows: the Start menu's; macOS: the Applications folders'), by the names app_open takes.

tools.name: app_open
tools.description: Opens an app by its app_list name, a file or folder (with the app the person opens it with), or a web address, as the person would. Its window may take a moment: wait_for, then screenshot.

name.description: An app's name from app_list (any case), a full path, or an address.

args.description: What to pass the app, if anything.

tools.name: app_quit
tools.description: Quits an app as the person would (closing its windows: it may ask about unsaved work), or ends it outright with force. Name it by its program (the app field of windows, e.g. notepad) or pass one program's pid. Waits up to 5 seconds and says what still runs.

name.description: Its program's name, with or without .exe.

pid.description: One program, instead of a name.

force.description: End it without asking it (unsaved work is lost).

tools.name: ui_tree
tools.description: A window's controls as its app describes them to accessibility tools: each element's id, role (button, edit, list_item...), name, value, position and size in screen coordinates, and its children. Cheaper and surer than reading a screenshot for apps that describe themselves; some (games, some web content) describe little. truncated says when elements were left out: ask for less depth, or a larger max_nodes.

window.description: The window's id, as windows lists it.

depth.description: How many levels below the window (default 12, at most 30).

tools.name: ui_act
tools.description: Acts on one element ui_tree listed, by what it is rather than where it shows: invoke (what clicking it does: a button, a link, a menu item), toggle, expand, collapse, select (an item of a list, a tab), focus, or set_value (the text of a box). An element that does not take the action says so; then click it instead.

window.description: The window's id, as windows lists it.

element.description: The element's id, as ui_tree gave it.

value.description: set_value: what to put in it.
